Muksun populations in Siberian river systems exhibit a maximum recorded adult total length of 90 centimeters [Li = 90 centimeters], a value derived from extensive gillnet surveys conducted over several decades in the lower Ob River basin. These large-bodied whitefish are slow-growing and late-maturing compared to many coregonids, a life-history strategy shaped by the cold, unproductive waters of their Arctic and subarctic habitats. In contrast to the ultimate length, the total length at puberty for females is substantially smaller, measured at 46.3 centimeters [Lp = 46.3 centimeters]. This size threshold corresponds roughly to the point at which vitellogenesis becomes histologically detectable, and it marks the transition from the sub-adult phase to reproductive competence. Females of Coregonus muksun are believed to reach this size between their sixth and eighth year, depending on local thermal conditions and food availability. The disparity between length at puberty and ultimate length indicates a prolonged adult growth phase, allowing individuals to continue increasing in body size well after the onset of gonadal activity, a pattern commonly observed in cold-water, iteroparous salmonids.

The incubation period of Coregonus muksun eggs is highly temperature-dependent, with hatching occurring after an average of 165 days [ab = 165 days] when embryos are maintained at a constant 1.5 °C [T = 1.5 °C]. This protracted embryonic development, which falls within the reported range of 150 to 180 days for coregonids, reflects the metabolic constraints imposed by near-freezing incubation temperatures typical of the species' spawning grounds in late autumn and winter. Newly emerged yolk-sac larvae are extremely small, with an initial wet weight at birth of approximately 0.0018 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.0018 grams], a value derived from the mean egg diameter of 1.5 millimeters observed in ripe ova from the Pur River system. These minute hatchlings remain entirely dependent on endogenous yolk reserves for the first several weeks of life, gradually absorbing the yolk sac before transitioning to exogenous feeding. The combination of prolonged incubation and minimal size at hatching is common among coregonids that spawn in autumn, as it ensures that yolk depletion coincides with the spring plankton bloom, when suitable prey items become abundant in the water column.

Under typical thermal conditions experienced by adult Coregonus muksun during the active growing season (13 °C [T = 13 °C]), the species' maximum reproductive output is substantial. Gravid females produce an average of approximately 12,100 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 12,100 eggs per spawning event], based on fecundity estimates from the Lena River population, and most individuals spawn approximately 3 times per year [F_R_i = approximately 3 times per year]. This reproductive schedule categorizes Muksun as an iteroparous, annual spawner with moderate fecundity relative to other large-bodied whitefishes. The same thermal regime of 13 °C also corresponds to the species' estimated maximum lifespan, with the oldest known individuals reaching an age of 23 years [am = 23 years] at a temperature of 13 °C [T = 13 °C]. This longevity is comparable to that of other slow-growing coregonids from high-latitude systems and is thought to be linked to the low metabolic demands and reduced predation pressure characteristic of these cold, oligotrophic environments.

Females attain a wet weight at puberty of approximately 1,000 grams [Wwp = approximately 1,000 grams], a body mass that is reached concurrently with the 46.3 centimeter length threshold and represents a critical energetic prerequisite for successful oocyte development. By contrast, the ultimate wet weight of 8,557 grams [Wwi = 8,557 grams] is approximately five times greater than the mass at puberty, suggesting several decades of continued somatic growth after reproductive maturity, a strategy that allows older, larger females to produce disproportionately more eggs and larger oocytes than younger spawners. This pattern is well documented in iteroparous salmonids, where female body size is positively correlated with fecundity and offspring quality. In Muksun, a female that reaches the ultimate weight may produce several times the clutch volume of a first-time spawner, underscoring the demographic importance of large, old individuals in maintaining population reproductive output.

Comparative analyses of body composition in Arctic freshwater fishes reveal that Muksun exhibits a relatively high condition factor, with adult specimens from the Khatanga River drainage consistently exceeding the predicted mass-length relationship observed in other Siberian coregonids. The asymptotic body mass of 8,557 grams [Wwi = 8,557 grams] is correlated with the high condition factor observed in Khatanga River populations, suggesting optimal local resource availability. Historical records from commercial fisheries operating in Lake Taimyr indicate that Muksun was once more abundant and attained larger average sizes than contemporary populations, suggesting that size-selective harvest has truncated the age structure over recent decades. Despite this pressure, the species persists across a wide geographic range extending from the Pechora River in the west to the Kolyma River in the east. Conservation efforts now focus on maintaining spawning stock biomass and protecting critical overwintering habitats in the mainstem rivers of Arctic Siberia.
